title: A day off
hook: Shabbat ends with a box of spices passed hand to hand; rest you don't have to earn
tomorrow: who stayed happy with one bowl of rice in a narrow lane?

segments.voice: Fatima asked for a servant and was given words for bedtime instead: goodnight can be a gift. Now, not one night, but a whole day off.
screen: `GOODNIGHT CAN BE A GIFT.` → `NOW, A WHOLE DAY OFF.`

segments.voice: A Saturday with nothing on it, and by ten in the morning the work email is open again. Rest can feel like something you're supposed to earn first. In Jewish homes, the day of rest, Shabbat, ends on Saturday night with a short ceremony called havdalah. A braided candle is lit. A cup of wine is blessed. And then a small box of spices, cloves or cinnamon, goes around, and everyone breathes it in. Why spices? Why does the end of a rest day need a sweet smell?
screen: `THE INBOX, BY TEN A.M.` → `HAVDALAH: CANDLE, WINE, SPICES.` → `WHY A SWEET SMELL AT THE END?`

segments.voice: Start where the Bible starts the rest. Exodus says that in six days God made heaven and earth, "and on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed." Even God, in the text, stops. Then the Talmud adds a picture. Resh Lakish, one of its rabbis, said a person is given an extra soul on the eve of Shabbat, and at its end the extra soul is taken away. Tradition explains the spices this way: a sweet smell to comfort you as that extra soul leaves. So the day of rest is something you'd miss, not something you got through. And here's the part for anyone who can't stop checking email. The commandment says six days you shall labor and do all your work. All of it, in six days? Rashi, a medieval commentator, explains: when Shabbat comes, regard your work as done. Not finished; regarded as finished. So in this Jewish teaching, rest isn't a prize at the end of a to-do list. It arrives on time, whether you're ready or not, and you're allowed to put the work down because the day says so.
screen: `HE RESTED, AND WAS REFRESHED.` · `AN EXTRA SOUL FOR THE DAY.` · `SPICES TO COMFORT IT LEAVING.` · `RASHI: REGARD YOUR WORK AS DONE.` · then, large: `REST.`

segments.voice: Find something with a scent near you: a spice jar, coffee, a slice of orange peel, a bar of soap. Hold it close and breathe it in slowly, a few times, the way the spice box goes around. Then set it down, rest your hands, and let the smell fade on its own. Nothing to finish.
A day off: in the Jewish Shabbat, a day when the work is put down because the day has come, finished or not.
Hold onto this: rest arrives on time, and you may regard the work as done, finished or not.
